name: Licochalcone A

lead: Licochalcone A is a compound from licorice root used in products for sensitive, red or acne-prone skin, giving calmer, clearer skin. It is also discussed for possible brightening through reduced pigment production.

Laboratory work reports antioxidant, antibacterial and anti-inflammatory activity, and licorice flavonoids have been tested for tyrosinase inhibition. Human data come from acne trials of moisturizers that combine licochalcone A with other actives, so its own contribution cannot be separated.

paras: It is used in leave-on moisturizers and serums for redness-prone or breakout-prone skin, usually as one of several actives in a daily routine.
The sources reviewed give no skin safety data. Wikipedia lists generic hazard labeling for the pure chemical, which relates to handling rather than finished products.

angle.text: Used in products for sensitive, red or acne-prone skin to soothe irritation and leave skin calmer and clearer, and discussed for brightening via less pigment. Human data are acne trials of multi-ingredient moisturizers.

lead: Licochalcone A is a chalcone-type phenol isolated from the roots of licorice species (Glycyrrhiza inflata and G. glabra).[1][2] In skincare it appears in moisturizers, sunscreens and post-treatment creams made for sensitive, red, irritated or acne-prone skin, and it is also discussed for a possible effect on pigment production.[3][4][5]

People use it to calm visible redness and irritation, to support acne routines, and to help skin look more even after procedures. Randomized trials of cosmetic formulations containing licochalcone A reported less redness in post-shaving irritation and UV-induced erythema models, and trials of multi-ingredient creams in acne have been run in several Asian and European settings.[6][7][8][9][5][10]

Laboratory research has reported antioxidant, antibacterial, antimalarial and anticancer activity,[1][11][12][6] and licorice flavonoids have been examined for tyrosinase inhibition.[3] Most human acne data come from products that combine licochalcone A with other actives, so its contribution alone cannot be separated.[7][8]
infobox: Soothing / anti-redness; examined for anti-melanogenic activity [3][5]
Ingredient in OTC moisturizers, sunscreens and post-procedure creams [4][5]

paras: Licochalcone A is found in cosmetic products for sensitive and acne-prone skin. A 2016 study paired it with 4-t-butylcyclohexanol, a compound that reduces TRPV1 activation, in a concept for sensitive skin and reported relief from stinging and a reduction of shaving-induced redness with a cream combining the two.[10]

Combination moisturizers containing licochalcone A, L-carnitine and decanediol have been used alongside adapalene gel, with intense pulsed light treatment, and as maintenance after acne treatment.[7][8][9][13] A sunscreen with an anti-inflammatory agent has been tested for pigmentation after picosecond laser treatment.[4]

In the 2006 study, licochalcone A reduced redness in a post-shaving model and in UV-induced erythema, and in cell experiments inhibited the oxidative burst of granulocytes, the release of PGE2 and LTB4, and the secretion of IL-6 and TNF-alpha.[5] The 2016 sensitive-skin work reported that licochalcone A reduced NF-kB signalling and PGE2 secretion in vitro.[10]

Six licorice flavonoids including licochalcone A were characterised in a 2013 study for antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activity.[2] A 1998 study reported superoxide-scavenging and antioxidative activity of retrochalcones from G. inflata,[14] and a 2005 study isolated licorice flavonoids and tested their inhibitory effect on tyrosinase, the enzyme that makes melanin.[3]

Licochalcone A has been reported to inhibit growth of Plasmodium falciparum in vitro and to protect mice from P. yoelii infection,[11] to disrupt bacterial growth,[6] to inhibit Helicobacter pylori growth in vitro,[9] and to arrest PC-3 prostate cancer cells in the cell cycle.[12] A 2019 review collects in vitro and in vivo work on licochalcones,[15] and a 2022 review of natural products that target cancer glycolysis includes licochalcone A.[16] Neuroinflammation and NMDA neurotoxicity have been examined in cell and mouse models.[17][18]

Licochalcone A has the formula C21H22O4 and is isolated from the roots of Glycyrrhiza glabra or G. inflata.[1] Chalcones are precursors of flavonoids; licochalcones A through G have been described from licorice root.[15] Licorice root has a long history in traditional Chinese medicine.[15] Wikipedia lists generic hazard labelling for the pure chemical, which is relevant to handling the raw compound rather than finished cosmetic products.[1]

In the randomized trials of cosmetic creams that included licochalcone A, tolerability was a measured outcome: in the 2020 relapse-prevention trial, dryness, stinging or burning and itching did not differ between the active and vehicle sides,[8] and in the 2016 adapalene trial the moisturizer group had less irritation by corneometer and water-loss measurements.[13]
The 2006 randomized, vehicle-controlled trials found that licochalcone A significantly reduced erythema in a post-shaving irritation model and in UV-induced erythema.[5]

In acne, a double-blinded 8-week trial in 120 patients with mild to moderate acne compared adapalene alone, adapalene with an active moisturizer containing licochalcone A, L-carnitine and decanediol, and adapalene with placebo; the moisturizer group had significant reductions in inflammatory and total lesions without flare-ups, with less irritation, and the authors concluded it reduced adapalene side effects without reducing efficacy.[13][7] In a 2020 vehicle-controlled maintenance trial, 50 responders from an initial 110 patients used a moisturizer with licochalcone A, decanediol, L-carnitine and salicylic acid on one side of the face for 12 weeks and had significantly lower lesion counts than on the vehicle side.[8][9]

A 2020 split-face trial in 29 volunteers found that intense pulsed light photodynamic therapy plus an active cream with licochalcone A, L-carnitine and decanediol cleared lesions faster than light therapy alone and showed a lower melanin index at one time point, with the authors reporting improved post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation.[19] A 2022 split-face trial of a sunscreen with an anti-inflammatory agent in 59 patients after picosecond laser showed a trend toward less brown pigmentation that was not statistically significant.[4]
These are all multi-ingredient products except for the 2006 irritation work. No studies found on licochalcone A alone for pigmentation.
